title: Why Are Orcas Sinking Sailboats? Scientists Say It Might Be a Game
summary: Picture this: you're sailing off the coast of Spain when a pod of orcas surrounds your boat. One slams into the rudder. Water starts pouring in. That's not a movie scene — it's been happening since 2020, and it's still going on in 2026. A critically endangered group of fewer than 50 orcas has been ramming and even sinking boats off Spain and Portugal, mostly in spring and summer when the whales migrate there to hunt Atlantic bluefin tuna. On July 23, 2026, orcas attacked a sailboat named Idem, striking its rudder until the boat flooded and sank. The two people aboard were rescued safely. Three other boats encountered orcas that same day — one lost steering and had to be escorted to port. On August 29, four orcas broke off about half the rudder of a 42-foot yacht, though all five people on board returned safely. Less than 48 hours later, a Spanish rescue vessel escorted another damaged yacht into the port of Baiona. So why are they doing it? Early guesses about revenge were quickly dismissed. In May 2024, experts suggested the behavior might be play. Bluefin tuna numbers have grown thanks to ocean protection rules, so the whales spend less time hunting and young orcas have more free time. Biologist Bruno Díaz López and his team at Spain's Bottlenose Dolphin Research Institute proposed another idea in September 2024: the young orcas may be using boats to practice hunting. Tuna can grow to 10 feet long and swim fast in groups, much like sailboats move through the water. "This is like a training toy," Díaz López said. "It's a shame that we humans are in the middle of this game, but they are learning." Not everyone is happy. In early September, Toñi — the 60-year-old matriarch of the pod — was shot with a pellet gun, leaving wounds on her dorsal fin. She appears to be healing. Scientists advise boaters to avoid orca hotspots, make loud banging noises, and swap smooth rudders for rougher ones to make boats less fun to play with.
why_it_matters: This story shows how easily human activity collides with wild animal behaviour: the same ocean protections that helped tuna recover may have given intelligent predators spare time to invent a new habit, and how we respond — with noise, boat design, or violence — will decide whether a critically endangered population survives.

background_read: The animals in this story live around the Iberian Peninsula — the corner of southwestern Europe shared by Spain and Portugal — and often feed near the Strait of Gibraltar, the narrow gap where the Atlantic Ocean meets the Mediterranean Sea. Since 2020 this small group has interacted with boats in the region again and again, and several yachts have sunk; the crews have been rescued each time.

The orcas are hunting Atlantic bluefin tuna, an enormous, fast, and very valuable fish that was once badly overfished. Catch limits set by ICCAT (the International Commission for the Conservation of Atlantic Tunas, a body of governments that manages Atlantic tuna fishing) have helped some stocks recover — which is why researchers think the whales now spend less time hunting and more time with boats.

Whales and dolphins can pass new habits around a group, the way children spread a playground game. In the late 1980s, orcas in the Pacific Northwest were seen swimming with dead salmon balanced on their heads, and the habit spread through several pods before fading away. That is one reason scientists are cautious about calling the boat-ramming 'revenge'.

Bruno Díaz López (a marine biologist who leads Spain's Bottlenose Dolphin Research Institute, which studies dolphins and whales) thinks young orcas may be using boats as practice targets, because tuna swim in tight, fast-moving groups much like a line of sailboats.

perspectives.description: If the behaviour really is play and hunting practice, it is a rare window into how orcas learn and share traditions, and a sign that tuna conservation is working. A recovering tuna stock and fewer than 50 surviving animals make every observation valuable.

For sailors, the encounters are genuinely dangerous: boats have flooded, lost steering, and sunk, even if everyone has been rescued so far. Continued attacks could push boaters or fishermen toward retaliation, as the shooting of the matriarch Toñi already suggests.

Animal populations sometimes develop short-lived fads passed between individuals, such as Pacific orcas briefly carrying dead salmon on their heads in the late 1980s. The early 'revenge' framing was a human projection; a habit spread through a small, related group is a more likely explanation than a plan.

Scientists recommend practical fixes — avoiding hotspots, making loud banging noises, and fitting rougher rudders so boats become less fun to touch. The long-term question is whether the behaviour fades on its own or becomes a permanent tradition, and whether protections can keep the pod alive while boaters stay safe.
